title: History of Milk — The Drink Most Humans Can't Drink
fullText: You've probably grown up believing that drinking milk is normal, that everyone drinks it, that it's essential for good health, that without it, your bones won't be strong. It's an idea you've heard since childhood at home, in school, and in countless advertisements. The problem is that this isn't true. Not because milk is inherently good or bad, but because most people on Earth simply cannot digest it. Around 70% of the world's adult population is lactose intolerant. In some regions, including East Asia, West Africa, and among many indigenous peoples of the Americas, that figure reaches 95%. And this isn't a disease, it's the biological norm. Humans are mammals and like every other mammal, we drink milk as infants and then stop. After weaning, the body normally switches off the production of lactase, the enzyme responsible for breaking down lactose, the sugar found in milk. Evolution decided that after childhood, we simply didn't need it anymore. That's how nature works. The exception is you. If you can drink a glass of milk without any problems, it means you carry a genetic mutation that most people on Earth do not. a mutation that didn't exist in any human population just 10,000 years ago. The story of how that mutation appeared, spread across continents, and eventually convinced much of the world that drinking milk is the natural thing to do is one of the strangest stories in the history of human civilization. But to understand where that mutation came from, we first have to understand where milk itself came from. And that takes us back 10,000 years to a place we now call Turkey. Around 10,000 years ago, in what is now Anatolia, a fertile peninsula at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, humans did something no one else on Earth had ever done. They domesticated cattle. The wild orox, a massive, aggressive animal weighing up to a ton with horns reaching over a meter in length, was gradually tamed and transformed into the domestic cow. It was one of the most dangerous experiments in human history, and scientists are still amazed that it was accomplished without a single metal tool. The first herders kept these animals for meat and as draft animals. They also collected their milk, but only for the calves. They couldn't drink it themselves. Physically, they couldn't. An adult living at that time who drank a cup of fresh milk would suffer from bloating, stomach cramps, and diarrhea because their bodies no longer produced lactase, just like every other adult mammal on the planet. Yet, milk was still an incredibly valuable resource, not in its fresh form, but after it had been processed. When milk fermentss, bacteria break down most of the lactose for us. Yogurt, keir, and the earliest forms of cheese all emerged because people couldn't digest fresh milk, but they could digest fermented dairy products. It was a remarkable example of intuitive biochemistry. They knew nothing about lactose or bacteria, but through generations of trial and error, they discovered what worked. And then around 7 to 8,000 years ago, somewhere in Europe, something happened that changed everything. At some point in a single person, or perhaps a small group of people, a random genetic mutation occurred in one specific gene. This mutation prevented the body from switching off lactase production. As a result, its carriers could digest milk not only as children but throughout their entire adult lives. On its own, this mutation would have meant very little if not for one crucial factor. The cattle herarding communities of Northern Europe lived in an environment where famines occurred regularly, grain harvests often failed, and animal protein could mean the difference between life and death. For someone with this mutation, being able to drink fresh milk directly from a cow provided extra calories, protein, and clean fluids when other food was scarce. It could literally mean the difference between survival and starvation. People with the mutation survived more often. They had more children. Their children inherited the mutation. Within just a few thousand years, a remarkably short time in evolutionary terms, it spread throughout the cattle herarding populations of Northern and Western Europe. Today, lactose tolerance reaches around 90 to 95% among the populations of Scandinavia, the British Isles, the Netherlands, and Ireland. These were the societies that had relied on dairy farming for thousands of years where milk was a vital source of nutrition. Now look at a map of global milk consumption today. The world's largest producers and consumers of dairy products are almost exactly the same regions where this mutation became widespread. That is not a coincidence. It is the direct result of something that happened around 7,000 years ago to one anonymous individual somewhere in Northern Europe, a person whose name we will never know. But while this mutation was slowly spreading across Europe over countless generations, milk was already shaping civilizations in other parts of the world in a very different way. Genghask Khan could not drink cow's milk. Neither could most Mongols as they belonged to an East Asian population with a high rate of lactose intolerance. But that did not stop milk from becoming one of the foundations of the Mongol war machine which built the largest contiguous land empire in history. The Mongols simply drank a different kind of milk and in a different form. Kumis or fermented mayor's milk was a staple of the Mongol warriors diet during centuries of military campaigns. As the milk fermentss, most of its lactose is broken down, making it digestible even for people who are lactose intolerant. At the same time, it contains alcohol, protein, B vitamins, and enough calories to sustain an army on the move. A Mongol horseman could ride for days while living almost entirely on kumis and the blood of his horse, making a small incision in the animals neck to drink a limited amount of blood before washing it down with fermented milk. It sounds brutal, but from the perspective of military logistics, it was a brilliant strategy. An army that carries its food with it, in this case on its horses, does not depend on supply lines. It cannot easily be cut off from provisions, starved during a siege, or stopped by destroying warehouses. The Mongol cavalry moved faster than any other army of its time precisely because it did not need long supply trains. Mar's milk helped make that possible. Today, kumis is still consumed across central Asia and Mongolia. It remains one of the few dairy products with an unbroken tradition stretching back thousands of years, surviving every major political and cultural transformation the region has experienced. By the middle of the 19th century, milk had become a serious problem in the Western world. Not because there wasn't enough of it, but because it was killing people. New York in the 1850s was growing at a staggering pace. Thousands of immigrants arrived every week and dairy farms could no longer keep up with demand. Enterprising businessmen came up with a solution. They created what became known as swill dairies. Dairy farms attached to urban distilleries. The cows were fed swill, the hot waste left over from grain distillation. It was cheap, abundant, and it made the animals desperately sick. Cows kept on this diet produced bluish milk with a sour smell. The milk was then diluted with water, whitened with chalk, sweetened with molasses, thickened with eggs, and sold as fresh country milk at full price. Children died by the thousands. During the hot summer months, infant mortality from gastrointestinal diseases in New York reached horrifying levels, and contaminated milk was one of the leading causes. In 1858, journalist Frank Leslie investigated the swill dairy industry and published a series of articles illustrated with images of diseased cows and detailed descriptions of how the milk was produced. The public outrage was enormous, but the dairy industry was powerful enough to block meaningful legislation for decades. The solution ultimately came not from politics, but from science. In the 1860s, Louisie Pastur demonstrated that diseases are caused by microorganisms and that heating liquids to a specific temperature could destroy those microorganisms without ruining the product. Pasteurization of milk was first adopted in Europe and later in the United States. Almost immediately, deaths from gastrointestinal diseases among children began to decline dramatically. It became one of the greatest public health victories in history. Yet, opponents fought pasteurization at every step, arguing that heated milk lost its nutritional value and that producers were simply using pasteurization to hide poor quality milk. Some of those arguments sound remarkably familiar today. The raw milk movement still exists, and in countries where raw milk is legally sold, it continues to contribute to outbreaks of illnesses such as salmonella. In the 20th century, milk stopped being just food and became politics. Across much of the Western world, governments introduced school milk programs that provided every child with a free or subsidized glass of milk each school day. In the United Kingdom, the program ran from 1946 until 1971 when education secretary Margaret Thatcher abolished it as part of a series of budget cuts. The decision earned her the nickname Milk Snatcher, a label that followed her throughout her political career. In the United States, the dairy lobby successfully secured milk's place in the government's official dietary guidelines as an essential daily food. For decades, those recommendations hung in classrooms across the country as part of the famous food pyramid. Advertising campaigns featuring celebrities with milk mustaches cost hundreds of millions of dollars and were funded by dairy producers themselves with government support. Got milk? One of the most recognizable advertising slogans of the 20th century was created within this system. The problem is that the scientific evidence behind many of these recommendations was far weaker than their supporters were willing to admit. The claim that milk is essential for healthy bones is challenged by data from countries with relatively low dairy consumption such as Japan, China, and many African nations, where osteoporosis occurs at rates no higher and in some cases even lower than in countries where milk consumption is much higher. Calcium is found in many foods besides milk. But for decades, evidence like this struggled to break through the enormous influence of the dairy industry's advertising campaigns and political lobbying. And then something happened that the dairy industry never saw coming. Consumers began walking away. Not because science had suddenly convinced them, but because they finally had a choice. Soy milk had existed in Asia for thousands of years, but in western markets, it remained a niche product used mostly by people with dairy allergies. Everything changed in the 2000s when advances in food technology made oat, almond, coconut, and rice milk taste better, last longer, and become affordable enough for the mass market. The Swedish company Oatley, founded in 1994 on university research into turning oats into a milk-like beverage through enzyatic processing, grew into a multi-billion dollar business by the 2020s and essentially created the global oat milk market from scratch. Over the past decade, cow's milk consumption has steadily declined across most developed countries. The dairy industry has responded with lawsuits, lobbying efforts to restrict the use of the word milk for plant-based drinks, and massive public relations campaigns. But the person who ordered a cappuccino with regular milk in 1990 and orders it with oat milk today rarely switches back. This is not the end of milk. Global dairy production continues to grow, driven by expanding markets in India, China, and many African countries. Today, the worldwide dairy industry is worth roughly $900 billion a year. But its monopoly over what is considered the normal drink for adults. The monopoly it maintained through much of the 20th century with the help of government programs and official dietary guidelines has come to an end. The journey of milk stretches from a random genetic mutation in a single unnamed person living in Northern Europe 7,000 years ago to a $900 billion global industry, daily school milk programs, the deaths of New York infants, Mongol horsemen sustained by fermented mayor's milk, and advertising scandals featuring celebrities with milk mustaches. It is the story of how a biological accident became a cultural norm. How that norm was embraced by governments and industry until it was presented as an essential part of a healthy lifestyle. And how the 70% of the world's population for whom that norm was never truly normal eventually gained the freedom to choose something else. The unnamed individual who carried that mutation in Northern Europe had no idea that they were setting in motion a chain of events that would one day end with oat milk being served in coffee shops across the 21st century. But that is exactly what happened. There is one country that completely breaks any simple theory about milk and genetics. India. In terms of lactose intolerance, Indians are genetically much closer to other Asian populations than to Europeans. A large share of the population has difficulty digesting fresh milk. Yet, India is the world's largest producer of milk, larger than the United States and larger than all of Europe combined. And milk occupies a place in Indian culture so central that even Scandinavian countries where more than 90% of the population can digest lactose have nothing quite like it. The explanation for this apparent contradiction lies not in biology but in religion and in the form milk takes before it reaches the table. In Hinduism, the cow is considered a sacred animal. It must not be slaughtered. Its meat must not be eaten and its very existence is regarded as a gift from the gods. Within this belief system, cow's milk is not merely a nutritious food, but a substance associated with spiritual purity. Panchcha gavia, a mixture of five products derived from the cow, including milk, yogurt, and clarified butter, has been used in religious rituals for thousands of years. Ghee or clarified butter is poured into sacred fires during Vadic ceremonies. Lassi, a yogurt-based drink, is served in temples as prasada, food that has been blessed and offered to worshippers. The key words here are yogurt and clarified butter. Most traditional Indian dairy products are either fermented or processed in ways that significantly reduce their lactose content. For thousands of years, Indian culinary traditions solved the problem of lactose intolerance intuitively in much the same way as the first cattle herders of Anatolia through fermentation and processing. Fresh milk is also traditionally boiled before drinking, which can slightly reduce its lactose content. Long before anyone knew what lactase was, genetics and culture had already reached a practical compromise. At the same time, the political significance of the sacred cow in modern India has become increasingly controversial. Laws protecting cows exist in most Indian states. Violations can result in prison sentences and in some cases they have been accompanied by acts of vigilante violence. In India, milk is simultaneously an economic commodity, a religious symbol and a political issue. all so deeply intertwined that separating one from the others is nearly impossible. While milk was becoming sacred in India, it was turning into something entirely different in Europe. The economic foundation of entire regions and the key to that transformation was cheese. Fresh milk spoiled within hours in a warm climate. Properly stored cheese can last for months, even years. For medieval Europe, a world without refrigeration and under the constant threat of crop failures and famine, this solved the same problem that the Incas solved with Chuno and the Mongols with kumis. How to preserve a nutritious food for long periods without losing its value. French monasteries played a role in this process that is difficult to overstate. Monks had the time, the discipline, the literacy, and the motivation to spend years experimenting with fermentation and aging. It was in the monasteries of medieval France, Switzerland, and Italy that many of Europe's greatest cheeses were developed. Monster traces its origins to an abbey in Alsace. Marwal was first produced in a monastery in Fllanders. The famous story that Rock for was accidentally invented by a shepherd who left his bread and cheese in a cave is almost certainly a legend. But the caves of Comaloo near Rockfall do provide unique conditions for the growth of the mold penicyium rock fori and monks or local cheese makers learned to recognize and take advantage of those conditions centuries ago. By the 18th century, cheese production had become a major European industry supported by established trade routes, regional reputations, and early forms of what we now call protected geographical indications. Parmesan from Palmer, Gorgonzola from Lombodi, Grriier from Switzerland. Regional cheeses had become brands long before the word brand even existed. Today, around 2,000 varieties of cheese are produced worldwide. France alone claims roughly 400 of them, enough for one different cheese every day of the year with plenty left over. Charl de Gaul is often quoted as saying that it is impossible to govern a country with 246 varieties of cheese. In reality, even at the time, the number was probably much higher. In the Soviet Union, milk became one of the clearest indicators of how the planned economy functioned and where it failed. In theory, the Soviet government guaranteed every citizen access to basic food products at fixed low prices. Milk, keir, sour cream, and cottage cheese were all part of that guaranteed minimum. In practice, however, the system struggled with chronic distribution problems. Milk was produced in one region and consumed in another. Transportation networks could not keep up. Refrigerated storage was insufficient. And a significant portion of the supply spoiled before it ever reached store shelves. Cues for milk became just as much a part of everyday Soviet life as cues for almost everything else. People lined up early in the morning. Milk trucks arrived at a scheduled time and their entire supply would disappear within minutes. Anyone who arrived too late simply went home empty-handed. Soviet milk cartons, the distinctive pyramid-shaped containers made from waxcoated cardboard, had a reputation for leaking and spoiled quickly, making an already limited supply even more difficult to preserve. At the same time, Soviet dairy science was fully competitive with international standards. Keir, a fermented milk drink whose industrial production was first developed in Russia at the end of the 19th century, is now sold around the world as a probiotic superfood and often costs several times more than regular milk in Western supermarkets. What was once an inexpensive everyday product in Soviet grocery stores has become part of a multi-billion dollar global health food industry in the 21st century. Few posts Soviet success stories are quite as unexpected as that one. If that unnamed person in Northern Europe who carried the mutation could see what happened next, they probably wouldn't understand any of it. A $900 billion global industry. 2,000 varieties of cheese. Sacred cows protected by law. Soviet citizens standing in line for kefir. Margaret Thatcher condemned over a single glass of milk, a $5 oat milk latte in a paper cup, a Mongol horseman crossing half a continent with a flask of fermented mar's milk. All of it grew from a single change in a single gene. From a random mutation that allowed one person to drink something their neighbors could not, from famine which turned that accident into an evolutionary advantage. and from thousands of years of natural selection, trade, religion, politics, and advertising. Each adding another layer to what milk has become today. 70% of the world's population still cannot digest it. The global dairy market continues to grow. Both of those statements are true at the same time. Not bad for a liquid that nature designed exclusively for calves. The journey of milk stretches from the pastures of Anatolia, where humans first dared to approach the wild oroxs, through the monastery cellers of medieval France, where monks spent years watching cheese slowly mature. through the slums of New York where children died after drinking bluish milk diluted with contaminated water. Through Soviet cues at 6:00 in the morning with empty milk cans in hand. Through classrooms where the food pyramid declared that good health depended on milk. It is the story of one of the most politically charged foods in human history. A product that has been at different moments a genetic mutation and a social norm. a sacred symbol and an industrial commodity, a safeguard against famine and a source of mass death, depending entirely on where you stand in its history. The unnamed European who carried the mutation had no idea what he was setting in motion. Genghis Khan wasn't thinking about logistics. He was thinking about conquest. Louis Pastau had no way of knowing that his discovery would save millions of children's lives. Margaret Thatcher never imagined that ending school milk would become the political label that followed her forever. The founders of Oatley simply wanted to help people with lactose intolerance. None of them could see the whole picture. They were simply taking the next step and milk kept flowing.
fullTextVi: Có lẽ bạn đã lớn lên với niềm tin rằng uống sữa là chuyện bình thường, ai cũng uống, rằng nó cần thiết cho sức khỏe tốt, nếu không có nó, xương của bạn sẽ không chắc khỏe. Đó là một ý tưởng bạn đã nghe từ khi còn nhỏ ở nhà, ở trường và ở vô số quảng cáo. Vấn đề là điều này không đúng. Không phải vì sữa vốn tốt hay xấu mà vì hầu hết mọi người trên Trái đất đơn giản là không thể tiêu hóa được nó. Khoảng 70% dân số trưởng thành trên thế giới không dung nạp lactose. Ở một số khu vực, bao gồm Đông Á, Tây Phi và nhiều dân tộc bản địa Châu Mỹ, con số đó lên tới 95%. Và đây không phải là một căn bệnh, đó là một quy luật sinh học. Con người là động vật có vú và giống như mọi động vật có vú khác, chúng ta uống sữa khi còn nhỏ và sau đó dừng lại. Sau khi cai sữa, cơ thể thường ngừng sản xuất lactase, loại enzyme chịu trách nhiệm để phá vỡ đường lactose, loại đường có trong sữa. Sự tiến hóa quyết định rằng sau thời thơ ấu, chúng ta đơn giản là không cần nó nữa. Đó là cách tự nhiên hoạt động. Ngoại lệ là bạn. Nếu bạn có thể uống một ly sữa mà không gặp vấn đề gì, điều đó có nghĩa là bạn mang một đột biến gen mà hầu hết mọi người trên Trái đất đều không có. một đột biến không tồn tại ở bất kỳ quần thể loài người nào chỉ 10.000 năm trước. Câu chuyện về sự đột biến đó xuất hiện như thế nào, lan rộng khắp các châu lục và cuối cùng đã thuyết phục được nhiều người trên thế giới cho rằng uống sữa là việc đương nhiên là một trong những câu chuyện kỳ ​​lạ nhất trong lịch sử văn minh nhân loại. Nhưng để hiểu được sự đột biến đó đến từ đâu, trước tiên chúng ta phải hiểu sữa tự nó đến từ. Và điều đó đưa chúng ta quay lại 10.000 năm trước nơi mà ngày nay chúng ta gọi là Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ. Khoảng 10.000 năm trước, vùng đất ngày nay là Anatolia, một bán đảo màu mỡ ở giao lộ giữa Châu Âu và Châu Á, con người đã làm được điều mà không ai trên Trái đất làm được từng làm. Họ đã thuần hóa gia súc. Orox hoang dã, một loài động vật to lớn, hung hãn nặng tới hàng tấn và có sừng có chiều dài hơn một mét, dần dần được thuần hóa và biến thành loài nuôi trong nhà cow. Đó là một trong những thí nghiệm nguy hiểm nhất trong lịch sử loài người và các nhà khoa học vẫn ngạc nhiên rằng nó được thực hiện mà không cần đến một công cụ kim loại nào. Những người chăn nuôi đầu tiên nuôi những con vật này để lấy thịt và làm vật kéo. Họ cũng thu thập sữa nhưng chỉ dành cho bê con. Họ không thể tự mình uống nó. Về mặt thể chất, họ không thể. Một người trưởng thành sống vào thời đó uống một cốc sữa tươi sẽ bị chướng bụng, co thắt dạ dày, tiêu chảy vì cơ thể không còn sản sinh ra lactase, giống như mọi động vật có vú trưởng thành khác trên hành tinh. Tuy nhiên, sữa vẫn là nguồn tài nguyên vô cùng quý giá, không phải ở dạng tươi mà là sau khi nó đã được xử lý. Khi sữa lên men, vi khuẩn sẽ phân hủy phần lớn đường lactose cho chúng ta. Sữa chua, keir và các dạng pho mát đầu tiên đều xuất hiện do con người không thể tiêu hóa được sữa tươi, nhưng họ có thể tiêu hóa các sản phẩm sữa lên men. Đó là một ví dụ đáng chú ý về hóa sinh trực quan. Họ không biết gì về lactose hoặc vi khuẩn, nhưng trải qua nhiều thế hệ thử và sai, họ đã khám phá ra điều gì có hiệu quả. Và rồi khoảng 7 đến 8.000 năm trước, ở đâu đó ở Châu Âu, đã xảy ra chuyện đã thay đổi mọi thứ. Tại một thời điểm nào đó ở một người, hoặc có thể là một nhóm nhỏ người, một đột biến di truyền ngẫu nhiên xảy ra ở một gen cụ thể. Đột biến này ngăn cơ thể ngừng sản xuất lactase. Kết quả là người mang nó có thể tiêu hóa sữa không chỉ khi còn nhỏ mà trong suốt toàn bộ cuộc đời trưởng thành của họ. Bản thân sự đột biến này sẽ chẳng có ý nghĩa gì nếu không có yếu tố quan trọng. Các cộng đồng chăn nuôi gia súc ở Bắc Âu sống trong môi trường xảy ra nạn đói thường xuyên, thu hoạch ngũ cốc thường thất bại và protein động vật có thể tạo ra sự khác biệt giữa cuộc sống và cái chết. Đối với người mang đột biến này, có thể uống sữa tươi trực tiếp từ bò cung cấp thêm calo, protein và chất lỏng sạch khi các thực phẩm khác khan hiếm. Nó có thể có nghĩa đen là sự khác biệt giữa sống sót và chết đói. Những người có đột biến sống sót thường xuyên hơn. Họ có thêm con. Con cái của họ được thừa hưởng đột biến. Chỉ trong vòng vài nghìn năm, một khoảng thời gian cực kỳ ngắn xét về mặt tiến hóa, nó lan rộng khắp các quần thể chăn nuôi gia súc ở Bắc và Tây Âu. Ngày nay, khả năng dung nạp lactose đạt khoảng 90 đến 95% trong dân số Scandinavia, Quần đảo Anh, Hà Lan và Ireland. Đây là những xã hội đã dựa vào chăn nuôi bò sữa hàng nghìn năm nơi sữa là nguồn dinh dưỡng quan trọng. Bây giờ hãy nhìn vào bản đồ tiêu thụ sữa toàn cầu ngày nay. Các nhà sản xuất và tiêu thụ các sản phẩm sữa lớn nhất thế giới gần như giống hệt nhau những vùng mà đột biến này trở nên phổ biến. Đó không phải là một sự trùng hợp ngẫu nhiên. Đó là kết quả trực tiếp của một điều gì đó đã xảy ra khoảng 7.000 năm trước đối với một cá nhân vô danh ở đâu đó ở Bắc Âu, một người mà chúng ta sẽ không bao giờ biết tên know. Nhưng trong khi đột biến này đang dần lan rộng khắp châu Âu qua vô số thế hệ, sữa vẫn đã định hình các nền văn minh ở những nơi khác trên thế giới theo một cách rất khác. Thành Cát Tư Hãn không thể uống sữa bò. Hầu hết người Mông Cổ cũng không thể vì họ thuộc dân số Đông Á có tỷ lệ không dung nạp lactose cao.
